transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-05-20
Start: 16:00 PT
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Alicia Park (Redwood AE), Ramesh Patel (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (AstraLoop Head of ML), Liam O'Connor (AstraLoop Staff Eng), Priya Singh (AstraLoop CTO)

Summary:
- Intro walkthrough of Redwood Hosted API for chat and text generation focusing on streaming, parameter tuning, and retry behavior.
- Customer constraints: strict p95 latency < 300ms for short responses, data residency concern for EU, and KMS/HSM requirement for keys.
- Agreed next steps: benchmarks, pricing, share security packet, schedule pilot scoping.

Topics covered:
- Streaming behavior and partial-token streaming vs chunking
- Key parameters: max_tokens, temperature, top_p, stop sequences, streaming chunk size
- Retry patterns: idempotency, backoff, token accounting during retries
- Latency vs cost tradeoffs: batching, prefix caching, quantization guidance
- Security: SOC2, SSO/SAML, KMS integration, VPC/dedicated vs hosted tradeoffs

Action items (recorded in call):
- See metadata block above for owners and dates.

Transcript (timestamps approximate, transcribed by Fireflies, some words misheard):
[00:00] Alicia: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, this is Alicia from Redwood Inference, I'm the AE on this account. We have Ramesh from our SE team who will drive the demo. Could you do quick intros?
[00:12] Maya: Hi, Maya here, Head of ML at AstraLoop. We're evaluating hosted options for our in-app help assistant, main concerns are latency and PII handling.
[00:18] Liam: Liam, Staff Eng, I'll be building the infra side, we'll need some detail on networking and keys.
[00:23] Priya: Priya, CTO, mostly listening but will chime on timelines and procurement.
[00:28] Ramesh: Cool, thanks. Quick agenda — we'll show a hosted chat flow streaming demo, then go into params and how to tune for latency/cost, then retry/failover patterns.
[00:36] Alicia: And to note, we also have the Console/Optimize snapshot in case you want recommendations after demo.

[02:05] Ramesh: Alright I'll share screen — starting with a short live demo hitting the Redwood Hosted chat endpoint. You'll see streaming tokens come in as the model generates. Note that streaming chunks are immediate partial tokens, so your client can render progressively.
[02:23] (audio: screen share click)
[03:10] Ramesh: For short responses — like question answer two to three sentences — the p75 is usually what folks watch, but you mentioned p95 — Maya — about 300ms target. We'll talk through ways to hit that.
[03:30] Maya: Yeah p95 is critical for us, for live help. If it spikes higher users perceive slowness.

[05:01] Ramesh: There are a few levers: 1) model choice — smaller models are faster and cheaper; 2) prompt design and max_tokens — smaller context reduces latency; 3) batching and concurrency — careful with batching if you have hard latency SLOs; 4) prefix/KV caching — that helps when prompts share common history.
[05:20] Liam: Quick question — batch size tradeoffs, you mean server-side batching where you combine calls?
[05:25] Ramesh: Exactly. Redwood runtime continually batches short requests to increase GPU utilization. The tradeoff is that batching introduces a queue delay; we expose batching windows and max delay so you can choose lower queue time for lower throughput.

[07:00] Ramesh: Also there's an 'early termination' mode: you can stream first token quickly by prioritizing short sequences — we call it fast-path. It's useful for short answers.
[07:14] Maya: That sounds promising. Does that require a different model?
[07:18] Ramesh: Not necessarily, it's runtime config. For example, lower sequence-length kernels and attention optimizations help.

[09:30] Ramesh: Now parameters — quick run-through: max_tokens, temperature, top_p, penalty params, stop sequences. For deterministic answers keep temp low and top_p low. If you're generating help suggestions, small temp (0.2) reduces hallucination.
[09:55] Liam: If we lower temp, do we see a cost change?
[10:00] Ramesh: Not directly; cost is per token. But low temp can reduce length of output which indirectly reduces cost if you cap max_tokens.

[12:41] (transcription glitch: Speaker 1) Speaker 1: when you do retries, how does token billing work, do you re-charge for partial tokens?
[12:49] Ramesh: Good question — Redwood charges per token emitted. For retries we have idempotency tokens; if request fails pre-generation we won't bill, if server returns partial generation then retries may re-generate but we provide options: server-side checkpointing of KV cache and de-duplication so you avoid paying twice for same tokens. There's also retry window and policy you can set.
[13:12] Maya: Can you explain KV cash — I mean KV cache — a bit more?
[13:16] Ramesh: Sure. KV cache stores attention key/value state between tokens so subsequent tokens don't recompute prefix. If you cache the KV for a conversation turn, replays are faster and cheaper. Sometimes the transcript shows KV 'cash' by mistake.

[15:00] Ramesh: Network & security — you asked about keys. Hosted mode supports customer-managed KMS via external key wrapping and integration guidance for HSMs. For stricter controls we have Dedicated or Private deployments in a VPC.
[15:20] Priya: Our compliance team requires HSM-backed keys and audit logs. How mature is Redwood on that?
[15:27] Alicia: We have SOC2 Type II and ISO attestation docs; we also provide audit log exports and SSO via SAML. We'll share the packet after this call.

[17:40] Liam: On network — can we restrict ingress to our IPs or do you support VPC peering?
[17:46] Ramesh: Hosted supports IP allowlists for API keys; Dedicated or Private supports private VPC peering and full customer-managed control plane. For hosted we recommend encrypting traffic and using short-lived keys and RBAC.

[20:10] Maya: One of our tricky cases is long context windows for an agent that has to see 8k tokens sometimes; cost matters there. Any guidance?
[20:20] Ramesh: For long contexts we suggest chunking the context and using a retrieval/embedding step: surface only the most relevant passages. Also quantization and model selection become important — you'll get a lot of cost savings moving from FP16 to int8 quantized models where quality permits.

[22:45] Ramesh: Let's demo retry behavior. I'll intentionally create a small simulated timeout and show automatic fallback to a lower-cost model and then to a regional replica.
[22:58] (demo noise)
[23:30] Ramesh: See here the runtime retried twice with exponential backoff, and we forwarded a 503 then served from fallback. You'll notice in the Console we show token-level cost and per-route latency.
[24:10] Liam: In that scenario, do you charge for the 503 attempt?
[24:14] Ramesh: If the attempt reached generation phase and emitted tokens, yes. If it failed pre-generation (e.g., connection refused) then not. We can instrument logs to correlate billing with traces.

[26:05] Maya: Is there a recommended idempotency token pattern?
[26:09] Ramesh: Use a client-provided idempotency key per user action. If you retry with the same key within the window, we ensure at-most-once generation semantics depending on policy. However if you have streaming partials, client-side dedupe logic is helpful.

[28:40] Priya: Timeline & procurement — if we like the pilot, what's rough time to onboard a small pilot?
[28:47] Alicia: For hosted pilot you can be live in days for a limited-scale test; Dedicated pilot usually 2–4 weeks to provision GPUs and networking depending on region. We'll tailor depending on the traffic.

[30:55] Liam: About region/data residency — can we pin to EU only?
[30:59] Ramesh: Yes, we have EU regions and can route traffic to EU-only endpoints; Dedicated gives you stronger isolation.

[33:10] Maya: Failure modes — do you have best practices for graceful degradation?
[33:15] Ramesh: Yes, common patterns: 1) fallback to a smaller model or canned responses; 2) surface partial content from streaming while continuing background generation; 3) queue and throttle upstream with sensible 429 handling. We also provide circuit-breaker configs in the Console.

[35:40] (brief cross-talk)
[36:00] Alicia: Quick note — Redwood Optimize can suggest batching/caching configs for your traffic and show cost impact. We can run an Optimize scan during pilot to find good defaults.

[37:22] Maya: Cost example — for our expected 200k requests/month what order of magnitude should we expect?
[37:31] Alicia: Rough ballpark — depends on model and average tokens. I'll put concrete examples in the pricing doc. We'll include token breakdown and options for committed Dedicated discounts.

[39:50] Ramesh: We're also going to share a sample benchmark harness. It will run p50/p95 latency under different concurrency and show token counts. That way you can plug in AstraLoop sample prompts.

[41:10] Liam: For the benchmark we will provide a sample traffic replay and a sanitized dataset with user prompts. Expect RPS about 30 with spikes to 100.

[44:00] Priya: Good call. As next step let's get the security packet and the pricing.
[44:06] Alicia: Absolutely, I'll send that by tomorrow.

[46:30] Mia (typo in transcript, likely Maya): Sounds good, thanks.
[46:36] Alicia: Okay I'll follow up with the links and we'll find a time for the pilot scoping. Thanks everyone.
[46:44] (meeting end)

Notes on transcription: occasional speaker mislabels and words like 'KV cash' instead of 'KV cache' present. Some technical terms truncated (e.g., SAML pronounced 'sam-el'). The audio-based notes are approximate.
